newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish trade officials on debt mission to Libya.
newsitem.headline: Turkish trade officials on debt mission to Libya.

text.p: A team of Turkish trade officials headed for Libya on Monday ahead of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's visit this week to secure Tripoli's outstanding debts of up to $365 million to Turkish building contractors, government officials said.

The treasury and foreign trade officials will begin talks with Libyan officials later on Monday on ways to speed up payment on the Libyan debts, mostly for projects completed before 1990, officials said.

"The payments that are due to Turkish constructors by Libya is something on the agenda for some time and it will remain as one of the agenda items that will be taken up during the talks," said Sermet Atacanli, a foreign ministry spokesman.
He told a news briefing that Erbakan was expected to meet Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi in Libya between October 4-6.
Erbakan will visit the north African country as part of a six-day trip beginning on Wednesday that includes Egypt and Nigeria.
"We are hoping that this trip will provide an impetus to our already existing economic and commercial relations with those countries," Atacanli said.

Few foreign leaders have visited Tripoli since the United Nations slapped an air and limited trade embargo on Libya in 1991 for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
The Turks were to fly to Tunisia and reach Libya overland.

Libya has always tried to increase trade with Turkey despite the embargo and wants Turkey to make the effort before the payments are made. Turkey, on other hand, would like debts paid before attempts to revitalise trade.
"Libya is able to pay its entire debt in a one-off payment. It is holding the payment issue as trump card in its hand to use against Turkey politically," a contractor said.

An official from the Association of Turkish Contractors in Libya (LTMD), based in Istanbul, said they would also join the mission to Libya on Wednesday with Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan to seek an urgent payment for a $200 million part of the total Libyan debt.

"The Libyan government pledged during the 1994 joint economic commission meetings that it would repay $200 million in three months in 1995, but never did so," a senior contractor from the association, who asked for anonymity, told Reuters.
The remaining $165 million, also from completed deals, can easily be made after the initial payment, they said.

Turkish contractors began giant infrastructure projects including housing compounds, dams, roads, fresh water facilities in Libya in the early 1980s. There are still some projects presently under construction.
Islamist Erbakan's talks with Libya are also expected to dwell on boosting bilateral trade, which rose to $623 million in 1995 from $498 million a year ago.
Turkey's exports to Libya are mainly textiles, cornseed oil, wheat flour and canned food. Turkey's imports from Libya are almost entirely oil and petroleum products.
Erbakan talked about possible fresh water sales to Libya two weeks ago when he unveiled economic resource raising package of his coalition government.
Officials said Turkey's state oil refineries company Tupras might seek to increase its oil and petroleum products purchases from Libya during the talks.
